strengths: Addresses a real gap in travel-planning benchmarks by introducing multi-turn interaction, unsolvable cases, and broader task scope (POI discovery, routing, flight/train search, weather) vs. prior narrow single-turn itinerary-only settings
Rigorous data collection: started with ~4,000 real user queries, applied K-Center-Greedy diversity filtering, and used dual-model solvability verification (more robust than single-model labeling)
Reproducible sandbox environment with ~100,000 cached tool-call traces and similarity-based retrieval for cache misses, enabling deterministic evaluation
Comprehensive benchmark with three evaluation subsets (multi-turn, single-turn, unsolvable) covering diverse dimensions of agent capability
Comprehensive model evaluation across 7 models with interesting finding that reasoning-oriented variants trade off unsolved detection vs. interactive planning
Well-written, clearly organized paper with clearly explained methodology and transparent evaluation protocol
weaknesses: Critical: Judge bias—GPT-5.1 is both an evaluated model (achieves 68.89 overall) and the judge/meta-judge, creating potential conflict of interest. Standard practice uses independent judge models. This weakens confidence in evaluation results.

Critical: Evaluation reliability not reported—subjective rubric dimensions (reasoning_planning, summarization_extraction, presentation, user_interaction) lack inter-annotator agreement study with humans and no comparison with human judgments.

Tool-call error detection (Eq. 6) only catches schema violations; does not detect semantically incorrect calls (wrong search parameters with correct tool/schema). Tool-error rate may significantly underestimate actual tool misuse.

Sandbox simulation quality for cache misses is unvalidated: no analysis of cache-miss frequency, LLM-based simulation quality vs. ground truth, or per-tool simulation reliability. Undermines reproducibility claims.

Limited analysis of results: no error analysis, failure-mode breakdown, or case studies. The interesting observation about model trade-offs (reasoning vs. unsolved detection) is underdeveloped with no investigation of underlying causes.
Data release plans unclear; paper does not state whether TravelBench will be released or under what terms. Without public release, reproducibility and community impact are severely limited.

Multi-turn labeling uses GPT-4.1 (a model) rather than human annotators; labeling scheme (multi-turn if ANY of 3 runs need multiple turns) may introduce bias. User profiles described as 'lightweight' but not detailed.
Unsolvable subset is small (~103 queries, ~2.6%) and underspecified: no per-category performance breakdown, unclear if dual-model agreement is sufficient, no analysis of failure categories.

Limited technical novelty: K-Center-Greedy filtering, multi-model labeling, user simulation, LLM-as-a-judge, and tool-caching sandbox are all existing techniques. Main contribution is domain-specific combination rather than methodological advance.
Missing human evaluation: no study comparing LLM-as-a-judge scores with human judgments, which is standard for published benchmarks.

No ablation studies showing impact of evaluation components (e.g., penalty scheme, meta-judge, tool-error penalties). Design choices like equal weighting of three subsets (Eq. 9) despite different sizes and difficulties are not justified.
Limited scope details: unclear where real user queries come from, no discussion of temporal/geographic coverage, appears English-only, no dataset demographics or bias analysis.

strengths: Addresses genuine gaps in prior work by including multi-turn interaction and unsolvable case detection
Pragmatic sandbox design with 100,000 cached tool outputs and retrieval-based cache-miss handling enables reproducible evaluation
Thoughtful data collection pipeline using K-Center-Greedy sampling, multi-model solvability verification, and interactive framework for task classification
Comprehensive benchmark covering diverse travel domains (POI, routing, flights, trains, weather)
Clear presentation and well-motivated problem
weaknesses: Critical evaluation methodology issues: LLM-as-judge relies solely on GPT-5.1 with no human validation, inter-rater reliability, or ground truth comparison; meta-judge calibration unvalidated
Shallow experimental analysis: results reported in Table 3 without error analysis, qualitative examples, or investigation of claimed model trade-offs
Missing ablations on evaluation components (e.g., impact of meta-judge, penalty weights) and no sensitivity analysis
Dataset scope limitations: 1,000 solvable tasks is modest; 103 unsolvable examples may cause ceiling effects; origin of 'real user queries' unspecified
Multi-turn vs. single-turn classification relies only on GPT-4.1 behavior; generalization across agents unclear
No comparison with specialized travel-planning systems from cited work (TravelPlanner, DeepTravel, ChinaTravel); only LLM baselines evaluated
Cache-miss handling via LLM simulation reintroduces non-determinism; cache-miss frequency and impact not reported
Limited statistical rigor: only 3 runs, no confidence intervals, significance tests, or standard deviations
Tool library (10 tools) has notable omissions (accommodation, restaurants, visas); no analysis of coverage limitations
Limited novelty: benchmark construction follows standard practices; sandbox adapts StableToolBench; evaluation methodology not validated against human judgment

strengths: Addresses documented gap in prior work: first benchmark explicitly supporting multi-turn dialogues, unsolvable request detection, and realistic tool use constraints

Comprehensive and principled dataset construction: 4,000 real user queries filtered via K-Center-Greedy diversity sampling and dual-model solvability agreement with explicit categorization of failure modes

Strong reproducibility infrastructure with sandbox environment and ~100,000 cached tool responses; clever similarity-based fallback for cache misses using embeddings to preserve deterministic evaluation

Sophisticated evaluation protocol combining multi-dimensional rubric scoring (4 dimensions for multi-turn), tool-call error penalties, and meta-judge calibration to address limitations of rule-based rewards on diverse domains

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 models (2 closed-source, 4 open-source variants) revealing important finding: penalty-adjusted scores substantially lag raw scores (10-15+ points), highlighting brittleness in tool use beyond plan plausibility

Clear insights about model trade-offs: feasibility detection and multi-turn interaction are distinct capabilities with models exhibiting different strengths (e.g., Qwen-plus strong on unsolved accuracy, weak on interactive planning)
Well-motivated and clearly written with effective use of comparison tables and straightforward presentation of methodology
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: sandbox approach credited to Guo et al. (2024), LLM-as-a-judge is standard practice, K-Center-Greedy is established technique; primary contribution is dataset rather than methodological innovation

LLM-as-a-judge evaluation insufficiently validated: only GPT-5.1 used as judge with no inter-judge agreement analysis, no human evaluation subset, no analysis of potential bias toward GPT-5.1-like outputs, meta-judge calibration guidelines underspecified

Cache-miss handling lacks thorough analysis: no reported cache hit rate, no ablation study on whether similarity-based fallback affects fairness across models, risk of subtle biases in simulated tool responses potentially weakening reproducibility claims

Multi-turn vs. single-turn classification depends on GPT-4.1 behavior (somewhat circular); dual-model solvability agreement uses only LLMs without human validation subset; no inter-annotator agreement statistics; source of 4,000 queries not clearly specified

Results section primarily descriptive with limited error analysis: missing examples of successful/failed trajectories, no detailed failure mode analysis, insufficient discussion of why models exhibit trade-offs, no analysis of tool-specific misuse patterns or task-type difficulty variation

Dataset size and documentation gaps: 500 multi-turn + 500 single-turn queries and only 103 unsolvable instances are modest; missing detailed statistics on dialogue length distribution, task-type coverage, geographic representation; user profile attributes mentioned but not specified

Incomplete methodological specification: exact prompts for user simulator (GPT-4.1) and judge (GPT-5.1) not provided in paper, rubric scoring guidelines lack detail, no mention of code/dataset release plan, penalty scheme weights appear ad-hoc without ablation studies

Limited exploration of design alternatives: no comparison of LLM-as-a-judge vs. rule-based scoring, no ablation on penalty terms, no reference solution comparison, linear 1-5 to 0-100 mapping justified without evidence

strengths: Real-world data grounding with 4 months of authentic user queries from a platform, covering diverse geographic regions (32 provinces, 243 cities), demographics, and temporal patterns

Novel three-task decomposition (Single-Turn, Multi-Turn, Unsolvable) that isolates three core agent capabilities: independent problem-solving, interactive preference elicitation, and capability boundary recognition

Implicit preference elicitation design where user profiles are hidden from agents during evaluation, requiring active questioning—reflects realistic multi-turn scenarios better than pre-specified preferences

Comprehensive reproducibility infrastructure: ~200K cached tool responses, embedding-based retrieval for cache misses, sandbox environment with isolated execution, demonstrated stability across runs (std 0.01-0.02)
Rigorous validation: Human agreement 95-97% across tasks, judge reliability (MAE 0.52 vs human-human 0.48), both dataset and evaluation framework validated through systematic human studies
Thorough empirical evaluation on 17 diverse models with controlled experiments (framework comparison, tool-calling support analysis) and clear findings about imbalanced cross-task capabilities
Clear presentation of benchmark advantages over prior work with comprehensive comparison table; extensive analysis of task coverage beyond itinerary planning (Discovery, Rules, Policies, etc.)
weaknesses: Geographic limitation is fundamental but inadequately emphasized: benchmark is China-only (Chinese language, locations, user base) with limited relevance to international researchers; geographic scope should be prominently stated in abstract/title

Limited tool set (only 10 tools) forces many practical tasks to be marked unsolvable; missing tools for real-time traffic, reminders, or booking create artificial bottlenecks that reduce practical utility and make 100 'unsolvable' instances feel like an evaluation workaround

User profile synthetic elements undermine privacy framing: gender, family structure, and lifestyle are LLM-generated, not real; only preference information is authentic; framing this as privacy-protective mischaracterizes the synthetic data injection

Evaluation heavily dependent on single judge model (Gemini-3-Flash); scores only comparable with this specific judge; no multi-judge agreement studies validating judge selection or exploring judge-model compatibility

Emerging ceiling effects threaten benchmark longevity: top models already achieve 72-76% overall (DeepSeek, Qwen), with single-turn/multi-turn approaching 80%+; paper's response about realistic difficulty doesn't adequately address saturation risk for future model improvements

Limited failure analysis: while paper shows imbalanced capabilities, it doesn't systematically analyze hallucination patterns, failure modes, or characteristics of hard tasks; restricts insights for downstream model development

Dataset scalability claims not empirically demonstrated: recombination of queries with different preferences proposed but not shown to produce diverse dialogues; 1,100 instances is modest by modern standards without proof-of-concept for scaling

User simulator concerns: fixed at temperature 0 (unrealistic determinism), asymmetric design (simulator has explicit intent, agent only noisy query), no validation of realistic behavior; no analysis of simulator failures

Methodology details: turn-type classification uses only 6 model runs per query; K-Center-Greedy diversity selection rationale unexplained; meta-judge only calibrates 3% of cases despite added complexity; no analysis of label stability across prompts

Incomplete comparisons: referenced benchmarks (ChinaTravel, TripScore) not evaluated on TravelBench to show comparative task difficulty; no cross-benchmark correlation analysis to position results in context

strengths: Real-world data grounding with rigorous de-identification and high inter-annotator agreement (95-97%)
Well-designed reproducibility infrastructure: ~200K cached tool responses with stable offline/online evaluation (0.11-0.31 difference)
Comprehensive validation: Judge-human agreement (MAE=0.52 vs human-human=0.48) with multiple runs showing consistent scores (std ~0.01)
Broader task scope than prior work: Covers discovery, navigation, rules, and policies beyond itinerary planning
Thoughtful benchmark design incorporating implicit preferences, multi-turn interaction, and unsolvable cases
Extensive appendices with detailed prompts and additional experiments supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: Multi-turn interaction, implicit preferences, and unsolvable cases are reasonable but not fundamental innovations over existing benchmarks (TravelPlanner, ChinaTravel, TripScore, Compass)
Critical geographic bias: China-only dataset (32 provinces, 243 cities) severely limits generalization to other regions with different POI structures and transportation systems

Problematic data preprocessing: LLM-based PII removal and synthetic profile attribute generation (gender, family structure) mix real and synthetic data; impact on realism unclear and risks stereotyping

Arbitrary labeling design: Single-turn/multi-turn split based on 4/6 threshold from only 6 runs; unsolvable annotation removes all instances marked unsolvable by even one model, potentially biasing toward easier tasks

LLM-as-judge limitations: Validation on only 100 trajectories; meta-judge triggers <3% of cases; no sensitivity analysis or comparison with alternative judge models; complex 4D rubric interpretation unclear
Limited analysis: No error categorization, failure mode taxonomy, or investigation of observed imbalanced capabilities across models; no analysis of which query types/tools are bottlenecks

Tool set constraints: Only 10 tools; many realistic scenarios marked unsolvable (real-time traffic, reminders); distribution skewed (map_search_places dominates with 105K/200K calls); no ablation on tool set size

Scoring methodology lacks justification: Non-standard normalization formula; multiplicative penalty terms can amplify differences; no sensitivity analysis; tool-use penalty only checks schema-level errors, not semantic correctness
Missing practical insights: No evidence that benchmark findings improve real-world travel systems; no correlation analysis between benchmark scores and actual user satisfaction or deployment metrics

Presentation issues: Dense 50-page paper with critical definitions relegated to appendices (e.g., implicit preferences in F.5); 8 pages of redundant prompt templates; anecdotal case studies lack systematic analysis

Reproducibility concerns: Results depend on specific proprietary model versions; manual curation steps create team-dependent variability; offline evaluation doesn't test real-world challenges like API failures

Incomplete related work positioning: Insufficient discussion of concurrent work (TripTailor, Compass, TP-RAG, Retail); no clear justification for why TravelBench is necessary vs. complementary to alternatives

strengths: Addresses real gaps in prior work with novel three-capability design (single-turn, multi-turn, unsolvable)
Rigorously grounded in real user data from platform logs with systematic de-identification and 97-99% label validity
Comprehensive reproducibility validation: offline/online consistency (0.11-0.31 score diff), low variance (std ~0.01), judge reliability comparable to human-human disagreement
Thoughtful methodology: multi-model feasibility annotation, K-Center-Greedy diversity sampling, 200K cached tool responses for deterministic evaluation
Extensive empirical validation: 17 models, meta-judge calibration (3.3% of cases), tool-use penalty, offline/online comparison, human annotations
Well-designed three-capability decomposition enabling focused evaluation of independent problem-solving, interactive preference elicitation, and boundary recognition
Strong practical grounding: diverse geographic coverage (32 provinces, 243 cities), realistic difficulty distribution, production-grade tools
Excellent reproducibility: published code/data, complete prompt documentation, detailed methodology enabling replication
weaknesses: Geographic scope limited to China reduces generalizability; while acknowledged as intentional, cross-regional validation would strengthen broader applicability
Tool set limited to 10 tools; some realistic scenarios marked unsolvable (e.g., real-time traffic alerts, reminders); acknowledged but impacts scope
Evaluation metric dependency on specific LLM judge (Gemini-3-Flash-preview); scores only directly comparable within same judge; alternative metrics suggested but not explored
Scoring methodology complexity (meta-judge calibration and tool-use penalty) could be more intuitively explained in main text; normalization rationale (Eq. 3) not well justified
Single-turn subset doesn't evaluate implicit preference elicitation (by design), potentially missing some preference-modeling capability gaps
Limited algorithmic or theoretical novelty; primarily dataset/benchmark contribution applying existing techniques (LLM-as-judge, meta-evaluation)
Multi-turn subset size (500 queries) may be modest for training large-scale models; scalability discussion limited in main text
